history: Pão is Latin panem, ‘bread’. Portuguese lost the final n but kept its trace in the nasal vowel: pão sounds as if the n were still there, and it comes back in the plural pães and in padaria, ‘bakery’. In the sixteenth century Portuguese traders and missionaries reached Japan, and bread went with them. The Japanese word for bread is still pan, パン, taken from Portuguese pão. In Lisbon you buy pão at the padaria or the pastelaria: a carcaça or a papo-seco, the classic crusty roll, pão de forma for toast, or broa, the dense maize bread of the north. Pão-de-ló, the Portuguese sponge cake, also carries the word.
historyEinfach: Pão means ‘bread’. It comes from Latin panem. In the 1500s, Portuguese traders came to Japan and brought bread. That is why bread in Japanese is pan! The plural of pão is pães. A bakery is a padaria.

elsewhere.text: Japanese learned the word from Portuguese traders and missionaries, along with the bread itself.
An English pantry was first the room where the bread was kept.
